turns.text:
Thank you for this opportunity to discuss Governor Hochul's Executive Budget and the operations of the Tax Department.

As I suspect you know, the national and state economies showed unexpected resilience last year, including slowing inflation and steady job growth. The Division of the Budget is now projecting a significant budget surplus going into fiscal year 2026, in large measure due to strong personal income tax receipts.

Still, we are facing very real economic and budgetary risks. Nearly half of New York's personal income tax receipts are paid by fewer than 2 percent of New York's personal taxpayers. Our economic fortunes are tied to their economic fortunes. When they have a good year, we see strong income tax receipts.

It's too soon to tell how the current turmoil in Washington will play out, but we know that uncertainty itself can impact the economy. We just saw an unexpected spike in the rate of inflation and a drop in consumer confidence. The president is using trade tariffs to advance both economic and non-economic policy objectives. And efforts to reshape federal spending and the federal government itself will have consequences for New York that we can't yet predict.

What is certain is that affordability remains an enormous challenge in communities across the state. Governor Hochul has proposed a fiscal year 2026 budget that is focused on addressing these challenges. As part of her Affordability Agenda, the Governor's Executive Budget advances several proposals to deliver much-needed tax relief to hardworking New York families.

First, Governor Hochul's Executive Budget would return $3 billion to New Yorkers in the form of a sales tax rebate. Under this proposal, the Tax Department would deliver rebate payments to 8.6 million households this year, providing much-needed relief to help families meet every-increasing costs.

The Governor's proposed budget would also cut personal income tax rates for low- and middle-income taxpayers. When fully phased in, the new rates for these taxpayers will be the lowest in nearly 70 years, providing nearly $1 billion in recurring tax relief to 8.3 million New Yorkers.

At the same time, Governor Hochul is proposing to keep the state's top three tax brackets in place for an additional five years, providing consistency and predictability in the tax treatment of these tranches of taxpayers.

The third prong of Governor Hochul's tax relief package is a historic expansion of the Empire State Child Credit. New York has offered a child tax credit for decades, but the credit only covered children ages 4 to 16. The Governor and Legislature expanded the credit in 2023 to cover children under the age of 4, allowing us to reach nearly 630,000 additional children.

We know that a refundable child tax credit is one of the most effective ways of helping to address the needs of children living in poverty. Building on the recommendations of the Child Poverty Reduction Advisory Council, Governor Hochul is proposing to decouple the state credit from the federal child credit in order to provide significantly greater benefits to even more families.

We will be increasing the maximum credit from $330 to $500 for children ages 4 to 16, and to $1,000 for children under age 4.

We will also be changing the way the credit phases out at higher income levels, and we'll be eliminating the minimum earned income requirement that historically functioned to exclude some of our poorest families. This initiative is a critical step in the state's commitment to cut child poverty in half by 2031.

At the Tax Department we're working to make these child tax credits and other valuable tax programs more readily available to New York taxpayers.

I have long been frustrated that low-income taxpayers too often turn to expensive tax preparers to help them claim the refundable credits they are entitled to under the state's tax laws. Exorbitant fees function to discount the value of these credits, diverting these tax expenditures away from the families they are intended to help.

This dynamic is one of the reasons New York jumped at the opportunity to participate in the Direct File pilot program last year. Direct File allows taxpayers to prepare and file their federal tax returns for free.

New York was one of four states that partnered with the Internal Revenue Service last year to pilot parallel direct-filing tools for state tax returns. Although the pilot was limited in scope and availability, 14,000 New Yorkers used the state filing app to prepare and submit their state tax returns for free, saving $260, about -- or $270.

This year, Direct File is bigger and better. More New Yorkers are eligible to use Direct File to prepare and file relatively simple federal and state returns. Direct File now supports additional types of income and additional types of tax credits, and the income eligibility limits have expanded to cover single filers with incomes up to $200,000 and joint filers with incomes up to $250,000.

We launched the Tax Department's mobile-friendly app when the tax filing season began in late January and, to date, thousands of New Yorkers have used it to file their state returns -- 83 percent in less than 15 minutes, and with a 97 percent satisfaction rate.

In addition to Direct File, New York participates in the Free File program, a partnership with tax software providers that allows eligible taxpayers to use tax preparation software for free. For many years we've run a companion taxpayer assistance program where members of Team Tax help eligible New Yorkers use Free File software to prepare and e-file their returns, building skills those taxpayers go on to share with their family and friends.

The team that built our Direct File app is part of an army of IT administrators and IT professionals who are replatforming and modernizing the core IT systems that power the Tax Department. We are now in Year 4 of this five-year project, still on time and on budget, and we're really starting to see the fruits of their labor.

We are currently rolling out a new wage and withholding system that employers and payroll service providers will use later this spring to file 600,000 first-quarter wage and tax withholding reports covering 14 million employee records.

This summer we'll be rolling out the new Real Property System Online, or RPSO, which will replace the outdated software used by assessors across the state with new, modern, cloud-based tools that will allow assessors to work more effectively and efficiently. We've been working closely with the property tax assessment community to make sure the new tools will meet their needs and can't wait to see the system go live.

This year Tax will also be launching Secure Choice, a state-sponsored retirement savings program for New Yorkers whose employers do not offer other retirement savings options. These employers will be required to make Secure Choice available for their employees, allowing those employees to use payroll deduction to save for retirement.

We expect to begin on-boarding employers into a limited pilot this June and, assuming all goes well, we'll be rolling out the program to all employers in the fall.

In addition to these signature projects, Tax is always looking for opportunities to improve our interactions with taxpayers. Many taxpayers engage with us online, including more than 7 million Online Services System accountholders. We handled more than 2.2 million calls in 2024, with 431,000 taxpayers opting to get a call-back instead of hanging on hold. More than 62,000 callers were assisted using interpretation services in 32 different languages, and we're currently working on changes to our integrated voice response menus so we can ascertain taxpayers' preferred language earlier in the process. In these and many other ways we continue to strive to improve the taxpayer experience.

As I suspect you can tell, I'm incredibly proud of Team Tax and the work we are doing at the Tax Department. I'm excited about the initiatives we are pursuing and look forward to working with you to move them forward. I'm happy to take any questions.

So we'll start with questions regarding the Executive proposes to make various changes to the income and eligibility rules for the STAR program, including proposals to require only one resident owner of the property to be at least 65 years old to qualify for the Enhanced STAR; clarify eligibility rules so only income of the owners who as primary residents reside on the property is considered; allow certain property owners who are not required to file income tax returns to maintain their benefit without the need to file income verification worksheets.

How many homeowners are currently enrolled in the STAR program? And what is the participation split between Basic and Enhanced STAR?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I don't have those numbers offhand, but I can certainly get them to you. And I know that we have millions of properties that are receiving STAR benefits. But I can get you the exact numbers.

Most properties are receiving the Basic STAR program. The Enhanced STAR benefits are going to low-income senior citizens who are property owners. I think the income tax -- combined income tax cutoff is 97,000. And we have hundreds of thousands of Enhanced STAR recipients and millions of Basic STAR recipients across the state.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYWOMAN WILLIAMS
turns.text: Has the New York State Assessors Association provided any feedback on this proposal?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I am not aware of any feedback we've received directly from the Assessors Association. I would expect that they would be generally supportive.

The -- one of the challenges that we have in the STAR program, particularly with regard to the Enhanced STAR program, is that the eligibility rules are incredibly complex and difficult for seniors to navigate. They're difficult for anyone to navigate.

We have a homeowner benefit portal on our website in our Online Services System that folks can use, for example, to enroll in STAR direct deposit. And one look at that, at the complexity of the registration process, will tell you that the rules around STAR are very complex. And they're complex in ways that I don't think are achieving the overarching goals of the STAR program.

For example, we're talking about the income -- you know, which owner's income is considered when determining STAR eligibility. We look at the income of both the owners who are resident on the property and the owners who are not resident on the property and their spouses.

And so, first, if the -- you know, I inherited a home with my brother, my brother lives in Arkansas, I'm the one who lived in the house and cared for dad, I'm still in the house, but it's not my income alone that matters here. Even though I'm the one who's in the house and still living in the house, we also need to try and measure the income of the brother in Arkansas and that brother's spouse.

The Tax Department doesn't have the ability to verify that income efficiently because that income isn't being reported to New York. So we're not effectively using that as a measure, and I don't think that measure is one that speaks to whether or not the occupants of that property, that home, are able to meet their tax obligations here in New York.

So by trying to ease that complexity, we think we will allow the Enhanced STAR benefit to reach the families that we want it to reach, as opposed to having people sort of default out of the system because it was too complex to navigate.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYWOMAN WILLIAMS
turns.text: Okay. You've actually answered other questions that I had, too, as to the barriers and so forth. And it's really great that you guys acknowledge that, because sometimes it can be very, very confusing.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I think the STAR program has become very confusing. It dates back to the '90s, and every couple of years a new situation arises and then we do a legislative fix to address that situation. And what we have done is made the program very complex.

I think it's complex for every property owner, and especially complex for our seniors. And I think our seniors -- we're providing enhanced benefits because we understand that our seniors are facing different challenges in terms of the affordability of their homes. And that mix I think is just not where we want to go as a state.

This will ease administration for the Tax Department, for assessors, and for property owners, and we think that this is the time to get it done.

Our chair, Senator Gounardes, from Brooklyn.

I want to start quickly with -- I have a bunch of things to cover.

But first, there was a proposal in the Governor's budget to eliminate the requirement that IDAs report the value of their sales tax exemptions to DTF. And they argued that it was redundant, a redundant reporting mechanism.

Can you comment on that? Is it redundant? And do you need that information?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
Yeah. So IDAs report certain tax-related information to the Tax Department, but they have much more robust reporting requirements to the Authorities Budget Office, including this particular sales tax exemption information.

The Tax Department is able to get that information from the Authorities Budget Office, either directly or through their online PARIS system. And so we have access to the information, but it is a duplicative requirement that requires IDAs to report separately to us from their overarching ABO reporting requirements, and requires us to process those one-off reportings to us differently.

We think we can be more efficient and it will ease a burden on IDAs without changing in any way how we oversee IDAs.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text:
Thank you.

And it's helpful looking at the tax expenditure report that your department puts out. It's easy to see that that exemption, for example, last year was $86 million in foregone sales tax revenue. Right?

And so my initial concern is without the reporting, we lose the finding there and the publication of that finding. And so even if we remove this reporting requirement, will you still be able and will you still publish that value in the Tax Expenditure Report as you guys have been?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: I think as a practical matter we're using the ABO reporting now.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text: I'm sorry?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: I think as a practical matter we're using the ABO reporting now.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text: Okay.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We receive it separately, but we can grab it from there in a one-stop that is easy for us to use. So we're using that reporting.

We get those reports from IDAs, and we could lean back on them if for some reason the ABO stopped operating. But I don't see that day. I think the ABO is performing important functions for the state.

And again, for IDAs, the sales tax exemption reporting to the ABO is one piece of a much larger set of reporting obligations that IDAs have to the ABO. So they're undertaking that reporting to the ABO in a different focused way than the one-off exemptions that they're reporting to the Tax Department.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text:
Thank you.

Going back to the Tax Expenditure Report, which I find illuminating, just a couple of weeks ago I kind of put out a quick analysis looking at some of the things that we exempt, some of the things that we forego in tax revenue, trying to total up some of the loose change that we leave on the table.

You know, found quite a bit of money -- you know, 3 billion-plus. One of the things that I saw in just the report that you guys put out this week, you know, we forego more than $600 million in sales tax revenue because we exempt people who buy gold bars from paying that tax -- $600-plus million, according to your estimates in the most recent fiscal year report.

Do you have a sense of who's buying those gold bars that we're giving that tax break to?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I think -- my understanding, although I've never gone to see the space, I probably wouldn't be allowed in, is that there are a couple of depositories for gold bullion deep underground in the city. And the ownership of that gold bullion may change on paper, but the gold bullion itself does not move.

And that makes all those transactions that are happening here in New York that could be taxable if we imposed sales tax on them.

We are taxing capital gains on the trading in that gold bullion, so it's not that there isn't a pathway for taxation there. But I think the historic rationale for this exemption, which was put in place long before I was involved with taxes in New York, is that it would be hard to move that gold, but it would be a one-time move. And they could relocate that gold to another state, and then all of the transactions about the ownership of that gold -- which isn't itself moving, it's not -- I don't buy it and take it home, it just sits there in the same place -- that a one-time move of that gold bullion out of New York would drop away all of that potential sales tax revenue that we think we might be getting if we remove the exemption, while further sort of diminishing the state's place in the financial services industry as a locus for that industry in the United States.

Our share of that industry is declining every year as the growth has happened -- you know, we're relatively steady in New York, but the growth in that industry is happening elsewhere. And I think the gold bullion here is an example, an artifact of some of our place in banking and investment markets. And if they figure out how to move it once, then it's over.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text:
Thank you.

Last year there was a proposal to basically continue a 50 percent -- I believe it was a 50 percent credit towards charitable contributions for income filers over $10 million. That's the only -- as I understand it, the only item itemized deduction that we let those high-income earners continue to claim even a piece of. I think the rest of them kind of drop off around the 450, $500,000 income level, they start to drop off at the itemized level.

Do we have a sense of a breakdown by income bracket who is claiming that itemized deduction?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: For charitable contributions?

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text: For charitable contributions.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I certainly don't have that offhand. We might be able to get that from our study files. I can certainly talk to our data analytics folks and see if we can figure that out. I would assume that we can identify that on our returns.

You know, I think this is -- we don't have the same limitations on deductions as the federal government does. But we have a particular limitation on these deductions here in New York. We also have some other provisions to make sure, for example, that we don't attribute charitable contributions that occur in New York to help determine residency here in New York. I think that's because we do have a significant sort of philanthropic activity in New York, and we want to balance the investments in, for example, our cultural institutions against the cost to the state of allowing those deductions.

That's a balance that certainly the Tax Department doesn't choose. But we can certainly try to get you information about that.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text:
Yeah, I'm just curious about the breakdown.

And similarly in that same vein, you know -- I guess you don't have this information handy, but I'd also appreciate follow-up on the bracket breakdown for filers who claim the college credit tuition deduction -- I mean, itemize that -- as well as the mortgage interest deduction.

Because it's my understanding that 90 percent of New York filers are not itemizing, and so I want to just get a sense of that 10 percent, what is the income distribution of that 10 percent who are itemizing.

And these are costly deductions. They might be the right investments, but I think we need to know who's getting these investments.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
Sure. Sure, absolutely. We can certainly try to get that information.

Again, I think that that will be a data analytics exercise against our study files.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text: And switching in the last couple of moments here, there's obviously a lot happening at the federal level right now, there's a lot of churn.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yes.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES
turns.text: A lot of churn. What -- with all the discussions around the renewal of the TCJA, what are you paying most attention to, what is the department paying most attention to with this renewal? What should we have on our radar as it relates to the impacts on New York's code -- where we've decoupled, where are we still coupled, et cetera?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I think we're looking at the non-TCJA provisions that are at issue most. I mean, we're certainly paying attention to the SALT cap, which has had devastating impacts on the state and state taxpayers.

But for the most part, we took action in 2018 to respond to the 2017 tax cuts, and we're in a relatively okay place with regard to those tax changes that are set to expire.

And what worries me are the other potential tax changes that could come together, especially last minute as final deals are being made, because we don't -- we didn't have very much time to respond to the 2017 TCJA tax changes, and that forced us to make some very broad-based changes. We broadly decoupled from a lot of federal tax changes because we didn't have time to have a more measured approach to those tax changes to decide which ones would work for us and which ones wouldn't. And then we had to go back the next year and the year after that to sort of fine-tune those choices.

And so if we find ourselves again where tax changes are being made without a lead time for the impact of those changes, we may find ourselves jammed with potentially significant changes to our underlying tax base because the federal tax base is changing.

So changes to the income tax base, changes to the appropriate tax base could all have flow-through consequence to New York if we don't just broadly decouple. And I don't think broad decoupling is ever really the right answer. We -- I think we want to have enough time to be deliberate in how we navigate the changing landscape in the federal tax code.

turns.label: SENATOR GOUNARDES

My question initially is going to be around outmigration and the implications that that could have potentially on us.

So the Governor is proposing the five-year extension on the increased taxes on the -- for the ultra-millionaire tax. And every year we seem to face troubling data on the number of individuals who are no longer here. You had mentioned in your testimony that nearly half of New York's personal income tax receipts are paid by fewer than 2 percent of our taxpayers.

Since these rates were first enacted in 2021, what is your office seeing in terms of the number of filers with incomes of more than $1 million per year?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
The number of taxpayers -- we call them income millionaires, or sometimes just millionaires. But we're talking about taxpayers who report a million dollars in income, not who have a million dollars in assets. I think that's very different and an important distinction to make.

We saw a huge uptick in the number of income millionaires in New York in 2021 because it was a huge capital gains year. That dropped away in 2022. I'm told that in twenty-twenty -- so we just finished our analysis of Tax Year '23, which are the returns that were processed in 2024. So it's also important to remember that there is a bit of a lag in that data because we're looking at returns that are retrospective reporting of tax income -- of income and deductions in behavior.

In -- I'm told in Tax Year '23 we had five more income millionaires than we did the year before, bringing us to about 86,000. And that trend again sort of depends on the economy in a particular year.

We have a lot of people who may go just above that million threshold or just below that million-dollar threshold from one year to the next, and so we can see variability. One particular taxpayer might be above and then below and then above and then below, depending on their particular tax situation. And a lot of our income millionaires are receiving a significant amount of their income through capital gains and other unearned income sources that vary with the economy in a different way than wage income tends to.

So we have a relatively steady number. We see outmigration of millionaires. We see outmigration of New Yorkers, net outmigration of all New Yorkers at every income level. There is data on our website, we have Tax Facts data, we just updated it this week with the information from the Tax Year '23 study file.

And I encourage you to go there and look at that. We have data, we have tables, we have charts, some of them are really colorful --

turns.label: ASSEMBLYWOMAN BAILEY
turns.text: Thank you very much. I did look at that, and it appears that most folks are heading down south. It looked like Florida, Texas.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER

We do -- I think Florida and Texas are certainly places. I think we all know people who have made that move to the Sun Belt for a lot of different reasons -- some for economic reasons, some because the weather's better.

You know, I think one of the things I found most startling is that we have net outmigration. We have people who leave and people who come in. Florida has people who leave and people who come in. We have more people leave New York than leave Florida, but that differential isn't huge. It's an in-migration problem that is driving our net outmigration numbers.

turns.text:
Thank you, Madam Chair. And thank you, Commissioner, for coming today.

How long have you been acting commissioner? You should be real commissioner.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: I've been acting commissioner for nearly four years. As I think some of you know --

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: Okay. I'm not sure why the delay. You clearly are qualified for this. So hopefully the Governor will --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: There are actually some retirement consequences for me if I moved into the commissioner role. And as I joke --

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: Oh, so you don't want to be.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: As I joke often, you want people with good judgment in a role like mine. And I would lose some significant retirement benefits if I moved there, and I just can't get there.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: I see. Got it. So that's your preference, then.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yes, absolutely.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text:
I see, all right.

I wanted you to talk about this new program that I don't know why I haven't heard of before, Secure Choice. So is that something that's going to be rolled out in Tax Year 2025?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We expect to roll it out this year.

The Secure Choice journey has been a long one. I think the legislation authorizing Secure Choice was first enacted in 2018, but it was enacted in a way that made the program untenable. The program as originally enacted was voluntary for employers, so employers would have an option to provide a pathway --

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: So this program is compulsory.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: It is compulsory --

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: For?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: For employers with 10 or more employees who do not offer retirement options. They aren't paying anything, but they have to make the program available to their employees.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: And will the state -- meaning your department -- keep track of the accounts, the contributions from the employees?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We have a program administrator that we have contracted with to be the basic administrator of the program.

If any of you, for example, might have participated in the state's deferred compensation program, that -- if you go to their website, that website is being operated by Nationwide, is the program administrator. It's responsible for the core accounting under the supervision of a board.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: So the employees in this -- participating in the Secure Choice program, would they also get the tax benefits such as --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yes, absolutely. It's sort of an auto-IRA program. We had to go back and amend the original 2018 law in 2021 to require employers to make this program an option for their employees.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: And do they get tax {unintelligible} just for New York State income tax or federal income taxes?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: For both. For both state and federal.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: I see. That's good.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
It is -- it is a retirement -- it's similar to a 401(k) or a 457B or other type of retirement program.

We think it's an important opportunity. It took a little while, again, to get it off the ground, but we have contracts in place for a program administrator and --

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: Well, thank you. hopefully we get this off the ground.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yeah, absolutely.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: Just a real quick response to one of your statements. You said we have a net outmigration --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yes.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: -- of millionaires.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Of everybody.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: Okay. But would you -- so it's a net migration --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yes.

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text: -- of millionaires? Because there are lots of millionaires moving to New York also.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: We have -- we have a net outmigration in all income categories. Except, I think, a couple of young people -- young people --

turns.label: SENATOR LIU
turns.text:
Thank you.

(Unintelligible overtalk.)

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text:
Thank you, Madam Acting Commissioner.

Assemblyman Otis.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN OTIS
turns.text:
Thank you, Commissioner. And thank you for your very thorough answers to everybody's questions. I think people appreciate that.

My question relates to a sense of the state of play in terms of cybersecurity threats and how the department is working with other state agencies to continue to protect us in an evolving situation.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
New York State -- the New York State Tax Department is supported by the Office of Information Technology Services. The state has a chief cybersecurity officer, and ITS is responsible for the core cybersecurity initiatives that are safeguarding state information, including state tax data.

We have -- we are subject to rigorous state and federal data security requirements around tax data. And we work closely with our colleagues at ITS to make sure that we are properly safeguarding that data. Those requirements aren't new, but they evolve every year. And I think our state cybersecurity efforts continue to evolve as the threats keep on changing.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN OTIS
turns.text: That's great. So you're confident that we're doing everything we need to be doing for the moment.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I am -- I think we're doing everything we need to be doing.

I remain always concerned that despite all of our best cybersecurity efforts, a careless action by an individual could expose a state system. And so we are constantly training employees at Tax around being cautious in their handling of other seemingly routine things. We train to make sure that people don't click on links, because it's easy to expose a system. And at the Tax Department we are incredibly focused on making sure that our employees aren't creating those risks.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN OTIS
turns.text: Thank you for that answer, and thank you for the great job you're doing.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.label: CHAIRWOMAN KRUEGER
turns.text:
Thank you.

Next, Gustavo Rivera.

turns.label: SENATOR RIVERA
turns.text:
Thank you, Madam Chair.

Hello, Commissioner.

You were cut off right at the end of Senator Liu's questions, but I was very interested in the answer. If you can tell us a little bit more about outmigration, in-migration, and some of the folks that are leaving, particularly since we hear endlessly about how tax policies make, you know, wealthy people run away, when there's many of us who believe that there's other policies that we follow that make it harder for working-class folks to remain in the state.

But tell us about some of them just in straight-up numbers.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
So I think the first and mainly main thing I want to do is I want to refer you to our website.

On our website we have a tax data drop-down, and that will bring you to what we call Tax Facts. And there are a lot of charts and tables around tax migration. One of my -- we have a chart that is looking at in-migration and outmigration rates historically.

Our rate of net outmigration dropped, has dropped in the last couple of years. We saw it really spike during the pandemic, which I don't think surprises any of us. But we are seeing our outmigration rates return to more historic pre-pandemic levels.

We did see a spike in outmigration of our highest-income New Yorkers in the year we increased our tax brackets. And then it dropped down to -- it started returning more towards historic levels.

I'm not in that tax bracket, so I'm not sure exactly why. But my assumption is that the people who were sensitive to those tax changes left and those who weren't sensitive to those tax changes are still here. And so they stopped leaving. They weren't sensitive to that.

We have also a heat map, I think they call it, that is looking at -- where you can see visually, based on shading, where the hotspots are for outmigration by age and income level. So we see in-migration for young people in sort of those upper-middle-class brackets, folks who are coming and landing their job in New York. And we see outmigration in most other age and income brackets.

But I think that that's a really good way to get a sense of that. And I really encourage you to look at some of those charts because I think that you'll find that really informative about where these changes are.

But again, when I look at the data, it looks to me like our rates of outmigration, while significant, have always been true. We have always had outmigration in New York.

turns.label: SENATOR RIVERA
turns.text: Tell me, just because we have so little time --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Sure.

turns.label: SENATOR RIVERA
turns.text: -- it's the -- which website again? Just because I'm --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: So if you go to tax.ny.gov, there's a tax data and statistics drop-down. And when you get there, there is -- one of the first things you get is Tax Facts.

turns.label: SENATOR RIVERA
turns.text: Got it.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: And you'll see a ton of charts and graphs and tables. You can view things as charts and as data tables. Take a look. It's great.

turns.label: SENATOR RIVERA
turns.text:
Thank you so much.

Thank you, Madam Chair.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text:
Thank you.

Assemblymember Miller.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN MILLER
turns.text:
Thank you.

And thank you, Acting Commissioner, for your testimony.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN MILLER
turns.text: My question is on the Farm Employee Overtime Credit.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Sure.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN MILLER
turns.text:
The Farm Employee Overtime Credit was the Governor's solution to keep New York State farms viable after the state implemented harmful, costly regulations on farm overtime. However, not all New York State farms are eligible for the credit, creating a dire economic hardship for these farms.

The Senate and the Assembly unanimously passed a bill last year to fix this so all farms would be eligible. The Governor vetoed the bill and instructed the Departments of Ag and Markets and Tax and Finance to work with the Legislature to put a solution in the budget.

Okay. Commissioner Ball shared with us that his department is working to find a solution. What is your department doing to find a solution?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We are also working to find a solution.

I think it's important to understand that the legislation that the Legislature passed last year was -- would not have changed eligibility for the Farmworker Overtime Credit. There were some technical issues with that legislation that meant that it would not have actually changed anything about the eligibility for the credit.

And that's because the credit is framed for taxpayers who earn their living from farming, who are farmers. And so although the legislation I think was intended to capture those farmers who use a separate entity to manage their labor costs, those separate entities aren't farmers.

And so where the underlying eligibility test is are you a farmer, that wasn't being changed in that legislation. And so that legislation was not going to expand eligibility for anyone.

I think that test of "are you a farmer" is an important one. It's been in place for a long time in New York across a range of benefits that are driven to farmers. But it gets a little tricky when we try to expand that concept to capture other entities that are providing labor to a farm, particularly in the context of overtime.

I expect that we will be engaging with your teams as part of the budget process when the negotiations sort of take off in earnest, and I'm confident we'll find a solution.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYWOMAN MILLER
turns.text: Okay. So I'll just answer the question: There is a viable path moving forward --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: It's a complicated one. I think it's going to be a complicated one and we're probably going to have some serious conversations about how to craft a solution that reaches those entities while ensuring that we're only paying for farmworker overtime that -- you know, for overtime wages that are being triggered by farming.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYWOMAN MILLER
turns.text: So do we feel that that's something that we can accomplish even though it's relatively --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yeah, I'm confident we can get there. I think, you know, we're leaning in, I'm sure Ag & Markets is leaning in, and I think we'll get there.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYWOMAN MILLER
turns.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

turns.label: CHAIRWOMAN KRUEGER
turns.text: Tom O'Mara.

turns.label: SENATOR O'MARA
turns.text:
Thank you.

Good morning.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Good morning.

turns.label: SENATOR O'MARA
turns.text:
Thanks for being with us.

An area that's been a significant concern of mine in recent years is the loss of financial services jobs from the state. I think in the last two years Texas now has more financial services jobs than New York State for the first time ever. Very concerning.

Even more concerning now is that the New York Stock Exchange has announced they're going to open a Dallas exchange.

What are we doing from a tax perspective to protect the financial industry that we have in New York State and the loss of that to other states? You know, it's about 20 percent of our total tax receipts in the state; 84 percent of that is from personal income taxes. So every job we lose to Texas is a loss of a -- presumably a high-income earner going.

So what are your thoughts on the loss of these jobs and the significant portion of our total tax revenues that we get from this industry?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
One, as I think I mentioned earlier, we certainly at Tax are paying attention to changes in the financial services industry because it is such an important component of the state's economy and a significant source of state tax receipts.

And to be clear, New York remains the center of the financial services industry in this country. But we're seeing growth in that industry in other states instead of in New York. And I believe --

turns.label: SENATOR O'MARA
turns.text: Well, they have more jobs in Texas than New York --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
Right, where those jobs are going in other places.

I think there's a combination of things. One, we enacted significant corporate tax reforms in 2015. We finally finished the regulatory process for that in 2023. It's been a 20-plus-year journey to restructure our tax code to align with federal changes that allowed for financial service entities to be engaged in activities that crossed our historic tax types. And so we combined them together.

Before those reforms, we were getting about half of our tax receipts from complex corporate taxpayers in the financial services industry on audit, because it was very difficult to fit their activities into our tax structures under the law. And although in some cases they are paying more in taxes, the certainty around the corporate tax law changes that we made I think are really making it possible for those industries to comply in a much more orderly and predictable way, and that that was an incredibly important step that we took.

turns.label: SENATOR O'MARA
turns.text: How can you take that position when we're losing jobs to other states and Texas has now surpassed New York on other jobs? That doesn't add up.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I think there are a couple of different things.

One, I think that we have -- in terms of our tax policy, we have made tax compliance easier for these entities. Although they in some cases are paying more, they are paying more in a predictable way, and that predictability is itself of value.

But there are certainly other aspects of our state's economy and the economy in other states that are driving these changes. Just as we were talking about people who are moving to other parts of the country for tax and other reasons, including affordability challenges, housing challenges and the like, we are seeing financial services firms make a calculation that it's easier for them to grow their business in other parts of the country than to grow them here.

turns.label: SENATOR O'MARA
turns.text:
Well -- and I'm running out of time and I thank you for your answers. And I've got one more area I wanted to get to.

But, you know, I think perhaps that predictability and knowing that they're going to pay more taxes in New York is leading them to leave New York because they know they're going to continue to pay more.

But one positive area, an area that we worked on the last couple of years, is reviewing the Excelsior Jobs Program. And the report and review of that showed a positive return on investment of $5.25 for every dollar invested.

And I'm glad we're continuing that program, extending it, and I think that's been a very successful program over the years.

But another one that was also reported on was the Film Tax Credit. And we get a 31-cent return on every dollar, yet we're continuing to waste $700 million a year on that industry.

Can you justify why we're continuing to spend $700 million on a program that has a negative rate of return?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I think you're referring to the Independent Tax Expenditure Study that the department commissioned at the direction of the Governor and Legislature.

I think that report itself took a very narrow view of the return on investment from our tax expenditures, and measured that return on investment only in terms of the actual number of dollars, state tax dollars that were generated by the state tax investment we made.

But that report made clear in the context of the film credit and other credits that there are intangible benefits to these investments that are not just metric in terms of state tax receipts that are generated.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text:
Thank you.

Assemblyman Ra.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN RA
turns.text:
Thank you.

We've talked about this issue a number of times. You know, we had enacted these restrictions a few years ago on flavored e-cigarettes. Obviously there is a dichotomy, I call it maybe even an inconsistency in the way we enforce tobacco and enforce these types of products.

And I know there are a lot of illegal products out there that come from China; they're not FDA-approved, so we don't even know what's in them. And I know you're not one to really offer an opinion necessarily about what we should be doing.

But, I mean, does it make sense to maybe consolidate the enforcement of both of these types of products under Tax & Finance? Because it seems like you guys have the resources and are out there and doing a good job, whereas DOH doesn't necessarily have that when they're trying to deal with these types of products.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
So thank you for that question.

The Tax Department enforces taxes. We have specific provisions in our tax laws that authorize us to engage in very specific kinds of criminal enforcement with regard to tobacco taxes and with regard to cannabis taxes.

We do have taxes on vapor products, but there are no enforcement provisions in the Tax Law associated with them beyond penalties for filing a late return and the like. We do not have the same kind of enforcement responsibilities or authority that we do for tobacco and for cannabis under the law.

There certainly are tax issues here. If a vapor product is being sold illegally, it's unlikely to be properly taxed too. But in order to have the Tax Department engage in the kind of civil and criminal enforcement responsibilities, we would have to be enforcing a regulatory scheme around vapor that doesn't exist in the law today.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN RA
turns.text:
Okay. A totally different subject.

The pass-through entity tax, I know businesses have been asking for flexibility on the election date. We have this proposal in the Executive Budget to extend to September 15th. But I have heard some concerns about this new provision that the election could be invalidated for nontimely payment.

Is the department considering these concerns? Is the availability of penalties and interest sufficient rather than, you know, invalidation?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We have certainly heard those concerns.

I mean, I think that the businesses that avail themselves of PTET have long been seeking to have the election moved to September from March because it allows them to have a better sense of whether PTET would help them.

I think it's always been a cash-flow concern for the state because that first estimated payment comes in March, at the end of one fiscal year, and moving the election to the end of September moves that payment into the next fiscal year. So there's a spin-down effect from moving that.

The language in the Executive Budget is the same language that we had in 2022 when the election date was moved from March to September. And I think the intention there is to ensure that we don't have significant disruptions to our cash flow by moving the election date.

I'm certainly open to finding ways to work through those issues with your staff and the business community. I think that's how we are trying to approach every one of the business tax proposals that we have and generally try to do business.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN RA
turns.text:
All right, thank you.

And then in December 2023, by contract, we had the comprehensive report issued on economic development tax credits. I know many of us have expressed concerns, you know, yesterday to Commissioner Knight with regard to a lot of these programs.

But I do note that the -- you know, we required, obviously, this report, but even the authors kind of commented on the overly broad scope. So just wondering if you have any take on whether a reporting requirement that we were looking more in depth at a smaller number, rather than trying to be so broad in looking at all of these programs at once, if that would get us better information as to the effectiveness of the programs.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
You know, I don't know if it would get better information. I think the challenge is in defining the goals for the investments we're making and then figuring out how to measure whether those goals are being achieved.

And I think, you know, at the end of the day the Tax Department isn't making these programs available. And so we can -- I sometimes -- you ask me about these programs and I have to guess at why we're doing them. I think that's where the challenge would lie.

turns.label: ASSEMBLYMAN RA
turns.text:
We do sometimes too have to guess.

Thank you.

turns.label: CHAIRWOMAN KRUEGER
turns.text: Senator Shelley Mayer.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text:
Good morning, Commissioner. Good to see you.

On the Enhanced STAR changes, do you have a sense of how many additional people will be eligible for Enhanced STAR under this change if it's enacted?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I think we estimate the total fiscal for the state at about $9 million in changes. Which, you know, about $1100 a family, is -- you know, there's some math there. We could figure that out.

It's -- I think the main point here is that the -- the eligibility constructs that we're using here are functioning to exclude people that I think we always intended to have be eligible for Enhanced STAR. And that complexity is deterring people from entering into the process.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: Yes.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: And so we -- it's going to be a very modest gain. But it will be a significant simplification for folks.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: Right. But you don't have right now the number --

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: No, but I could probably do it in my head.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: Co-ops will still be included, co-ops and condominiums?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yes. Yeah, we're not changing the scope of coverage of these programs, we're just changing like which incomes we're looking at.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: Yes, understood.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: What about the process of challenging a determination of Tax & Finance? Does this require additional staff on your part? And how long does the department have to make a decision on an appeal?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We handle those appeals expeditiously. It's not going to take additional staff for us. If anything, we expect that the number of challenges will likely go down.

One of the things that is certainly frustrating for us is that I think there are a lot of tax property owners who don't understand why they were not eligible when it was an income disqualification. And we're looking at their tax return, and you're not qualified, based on that.

So we don't see a ton of reversals of appeals of these eligibility determinations, because for the most part they're really straightforward. We looked at your tax filing, and your tax filing said this, and therefore you're not eligible.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text:
I understand.

But is there a requirement in your proposal as to how quickly you must determine -- from a consumer point of view.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
I don't believe so. I don't believe so.

There are -- I think there are a myriad of changes we could make to start to simplify it, and that could include some additional changes to the STAR program that I think would make the protest process more straightforward.

I think not consistent between the credit and the exemption, between the basic exemption and the enhanced exemption, because those laws have evolved at different times. And we could also strive to simplify that. You might see that proposal next year.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: We need simplification. It's extremely hard for an individual homeowner to figure out.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: It's very hard, yes.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text:
So I'm interested in that.

I have one more question. How much staff does Tax & Finance have?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: We have just under 4,000 right now.

turns.label: SENATOR MAYER
turns.text: Okay, thank you.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text:
Thank you, Senator.

I just have a couple of questions, Madam Commissioner.

The Governor is proposing a middle-class tax cut for certain taxpayers. It's a three-part question. First, who is not eligible for this? I never know who the certain taxpayers are. So who is not eligible for this tax cut?

When will it kick in? And will you be adjusting the tax rate tables this year, or is it next year?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: The proposal would cover taxpayers up through -- I think it's 323,000 for married filing jointly.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text: Right. Right.

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: Those tax brackets. So the tax brackets above that are 6.85 or 9.3 or 10 point -- 9.65 or 10.3 and our 10.9 brackets would remain unchanged. For taxpayers reporting more than $323,000 for joint filers, it's ties about 160 --

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text: Taxpayers under that, that max, that aren't eligible, who would that be?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: For the tax credit, those would be those taxpayers --

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text: So everyone that makes less than $323,000 is eligible?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
Yes, they would all -- the proposal is to reduce our income tax brackets by one basis point this year and by another basis point next year. The proposal would bring our tax rates to the -- to essentially the lowest tax rates since 1934. We had a zero rate in 1958, which makes it a blip. But otherwise we're going back to 1934 when we imposed the income tax.

The first tax rate change would be for tax year '25, for this year. The second basis point change would be for next year. That would be recurring relief going forward from there.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text:
Okay. And the Governor is also proposing a -- I think we're calling it an inflation refund that totals around $3 billion for people earning less than $300,000 -- taxpayers filing less than $300,000.

When will those checks be sent out to the taxpayers, do you know?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text:
We would be sending them out later this year.

I think the specific timing would have to fall around our STAR check mailings. We have some timing obligations under the law around when we deliver STAR credits as compared to their billing cycle, so we would be sliding these rebate checks in around that mailing schedule.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text: And what recourse will the taxpayers have if they don't receive a check by the end of the year?

turns.label: DTF COMMISSIONER HILLER
turns.text: These rebates are structurally income tax credits. That's how we deliver these kinds of check programs historically. And so they would have all of the recourse that would be available to them for any personal income tax matter.

turns.label: CHAIRMAN PRETLOW
turns.text: Okay. And just a back of the envelope calculation in your head, if we reduce the max income from 300,000 to 150,000, do you know -- can you estimate what that number would be? I know there would be more people less than than above, so it wouldn't be half.

The state does have currently a $6.3 billion debt to the federal government as a result of COVID. The state needed to borrow money because of the unprecedented amounts of business closures we saw during COVID that were mandated by state public policy decisions.

Those closures obviously led to a drastic amount of layoffs in a short period of time. The unemployment system was quickly overwhelmed. The state needed to borrow money to pay out unemployment insurance benefits. We still have 6.3 billion that we owe back to the federal government.

The Governor's Executive Budget proposal has allocated $165 million to pay the interest assessment surcharge, which NFIB strongly supports. This surcharge is assessed once a year on employers to just pay the interest on the state's debt. That notice goes out in the summer. Last year it was about $15 per employee.

We support the Governor's initiative to pay this -- for the state to pay this, because small businesses have been shouldering the burden of paying back the UI debt by themselves without any assistance.

This is contrary to what 36 other states have done. They used COVID relief funds to address their UI debt, to pay it off, to get it back to solvency, and to restore UI tax levels.

Small businesses are also paying $105 in increased federal UI taxes, they're paying $250 per employee in state UI taxes. This is a big problem, and New York State does need to address it sooner than later.

Thank you for your time today, and I'm happy to answer questions.

All right, good morning. And thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

My name is Kari Siddiqui. I am a project director with the Schuyler Center for Analysis and Advocacy, where I focus on our child poverty reduction work.

The Schuyler Center is a 152-year-old statewide nonprofit organization based here in Albany and dedicated to policy analysis and advocacy in support of public systems that meet the needs of children and families, particularly those living in poverty.

I'm going to take a turn from what we just talked about and talk about how the tax code can better support New York's kids and families. And this year we have a tremendous opportunity to make a real substantial change to our child tax credit so that it can better help and support children and families and make New York State an affordable home for our families.

Backing up just a tiny bit, in 2021 the Legislature passed, you all passed and Governor Hochul signed into law the Child Poverty Reduction Act, which commits the state to reduce child poverty by 50 percent by 2031. It also established the Child Poverty Reduction Advisory Council, which just this past December released a set of really strong recommendations that would help New York State achieve that goal.

And key among their recommendations was an expansion to the Empire State Child Credit, which is our child tax credit here in New York.

In January the Governor included an expansion of the tax credit in her Executive Budget, a proposal that, if passed, would be the largest expansion of the credit since its establishment, and one that is a great first step towards a stronger, more impactful child tax credit.

The Governor's proposal is broad-based. It reaches both our lowest-income and middle-class families and extends the credit to lower-income families who actually, due to their low income level, were previously excluded from receiving the full credit amount.

But while the Governor's proposal is a great starting place, we can and must do more to make our tax credit work better for families and have a stronger poverty-fighting potential. The child tax credit expansion recommended by the Child Poverty Reduction Advisory Council would provide a larger amount, $1500 per child per year for all children zero to 18, while still eliminating that income requirement that has excluded the lowest-income families from the full credit amount.

It's also critical to index the credit to inflation so that families can continue to benefit from the full value of the credit for years to come. The expansion that is recommended by the Child Poverty Reduction Advisory Council is estimated to reduce child poverty by 23 percent compared to an estimated 8 percent reduction from the Governor's proposal.

I will point out that the Working Families Tax Credit, sponsored by Senator Gounardes and by Assemblymember Hevesi, would encompass all of the changes in the CPRAC recommendation and go even further to put money into families' pockets, including by paying the credit out throughout the year.

I'll end as I began, which is to say that we have a real opportunity this year to start to make New York State an affordable place and the best place to raise a family. Research on this topic has shown us again and again that tax credits work.

Thank you.

So what's going to happen is right now we're at 1.2 percent in a FUTA offset, so that equals about an extra $105 per employee for federal UI taxes. So that's going to double next year if the state still has its debt. So we're going to go from 1.2 percent to 2.3 percent. So businesses are going to be looking at a sizable jump in their federal UI taxes.

They do this as a way to pay the debt off faster, right? So you're talking hundreds of extra dollars per employee per year.

So small businesses have poured out thousands of additional dollars to fix New York State's UI problem -- which again, to remind everybody, was a result of state public policy decisions. Right? The state shut down businesses.

And unlike 30-plus other states, New York just said, Oh, well, businesses, you're on the hook to pay it back. Other states used COVID relief funds to address their UI problems; New York hasn't.

And this is, again -- to the points that were made earlier as well, you cannot adjust the weekly benefit UI rate with the state's outstanding debt.

So the longer we let this go on, you can't do anything for workers either. You cannot -- the federal government will not allow you to increase UI weekly benefit rates as long as New York has this unemployment insurance problem. It's in the best interests of the state to address this problem now and to not let it continue.
